hello.note: Sounds like 'hi'. More formal: Goddag. Casual: Hejsa!

goodbye.note: In everyday speech Danes usually just say Hej hej! when leaving. Also: Vi ses (see you).

please.note: Quite formal. Danes usually just add tak to a request: En kaffe, tak (a coffee, please).

thank_you.note: Warmer: Mange tak or Tusind tak (a thousand thanks).

youre_welcome.note: Also: Ingen årsag. In shops the reply to Tak is often Selv tak (thank you too).

yes.note: To say yes to a negative question, use jo: Kommer du ikke? – Jo!

sorry.note: Both d's are silent: roughly 'ON-skül'. For real regret: Det er jeg ked af.

excuse_me.note: Often just Undskyld, followed by your question: Undskyld, ved du hvor stationen er?

good_morning.note: Casual: Morn! In Southern Jutland, Mojn is used as hi and bye all day.

how_are_you.note: Danes say du to almost everyone; the formal De is now rare. Also: Hvordan går det?

im_fine.note: Shorter: Fint, tak! To ask back: Hvad med dig?

whats_your_name.note: Hvad is said 'va'. The dd in hedder is a soft d, like th in 'this'.

my_name_is.note: Jeg sounds like 'yai'. More formal: Mit navn er …

nice_to_meet_you.note: Also common: Rart at møde dig or Hyggeligt at hilse på dig.

where_from.note: Also common: Hvor er du fra?

speak_english.note: More casual: Snakker du engelsk? Most Danes speak English well.

dont_understand.note: Handy: Jeg forstår ikke dansk (I don't understand Danish).

speak_slowly.note: Danes make polite requests as questions. Softer still: Vil du godt tale lidt langsommere?

where.note: The h is silent, as in every Danish word starting with hv: roughly 'vor'.

what.note: Said 'va'. Politer if you didn't catch something: Hvad siger du? or just Undskyld?

when.note: Stress on the last syllable: vor-NOR.

how_much.note: Pointing at something: Hvad koster den her? Also: Hvor meget koster det?

where_bathroom.note: Put Undskyld in front to be polite: Undskyld, hvor er toilettet?

can_you_help.note: The h in hjælpe is silent. Extra polite: Vil du være sød at hjælpe mig?

what_time.note: Also very common: Hvor mange er klokken?

what_means.note: Pointing at a word or sign: Hvad betyder det her?

one.note: With neuter nouns it is et: et glas. Written én when stressed, to tell it from the article en.

four.note: Two syllables, roughly 'FEE-ah'. Nothing to do with English fire.

seven.note: Roughly 'syoo'; the v is barely heard.

ten.note: Say 'tee'. Heads-up: from 50 up, Danish counts in twenties, e.g. halvtreds = 50.

water.note: The d is silent: 'van'. Tap water is fine to drink: Et glas vand, tak.

bread.note: The d is soft, like th in 'this'. Dark rye bread is rugbrød.

menu_please.note: For a group: Må vi få menukortet? Often shortened to kortet.

bill_please.note: More casual: Kan jeg få regningen?

delicious.note: Also: Det smager godt! The æ sounds like e in 'bed'.

no_meat.note: Kød has a soft d, like th in 'this'. Vegetarian: Jeg er vegetar.

enjoy_meal.note: Waiters say it as they serve. At home the host says Værsgo! before eating, and Velbekomme in reply to Tak for mad.

straight_ahead.note: The g is silent and the stress is on ud: 'lee-eh-OOTH'. Keep going straight: Bare fortsæt ligeud.

stop_here.note: The usual polite way to say it. Shorter: Stop her, tak.

airport.note: Copenhagen's airport is often just called Kastrup, after the area it is in.

hotel.note: Same word as in English, and also stressed on the end: ho-TEL.

train_station.note: Often just stationen. A city's main station is the banegård, e.g. Hovedbanegården.

want_to_go.note: Danes drop the verb go. In a taxi, simply: Til …, tak.

is_it_far.note: Also: Er det langt herfra? (from here)

one_ticket.note: Billet is stressed on the end: bi-LET. With a destination: En billet til Odense, tak.

too_expensive.note: Prices in shops are fixed; haggling is only normal at flea markets (loppemarkeder).

cheaper.note: I (plural you) means the shop. To just one person: Har du noget billigere?

id_like_this.text: Jeg vil gerne have den her
id_like_this.note: Use det her for neuter nouns. Also common: Jeg tager den her (I'll take this one).

just_looking.note: Usually: Nej tak, jeg kigger bare.

pay_card.note: Card is the norm in Denmark; many people also pay with their phone.

cash.note: To pay in cash: at betale kontant.

open.note: Also seen: Åbent, as in Vi har åbent (we're open).

closed.note: Closed today: Lukket i dag. Opening hours: åbningstider.

big.note: With plural nouns: store, e.g. store kopper (big cups).

small.note: With plural nouns: små, e.g. små kopper (small cups).

tomorrow.note: Roughly 'ee-MORN'. Tomorrow morning: i morgen tidlig.

later.note: Also: om lidt (in a little while).

good_evening.note: Quite formal; in casual settings Danes just say Hej.

good_night.note: Also said when leaving late in the evening.

see_you_later.note: Also: Vi ses senere. Casual: Ses!

wait_moment.note: Also very common: Lige et øjeblik. Casual: Vent lige!

every_day.note: The h in hver is silent: 'vair'.

call_police.note: The emergency number for police, fire and ambulance is 112.

need_doctor.text: Jeg har brug for en læge
need_doctor.note: Læge sounds like 'LAY-yeh'. Urgent: Ring efter en ambulance!

im_lost.note: Also: Jeg kan ikke finde vej (I can't find my way).

dont_feel_well.note: Also: Jeg har det dårligt. Feeling sick to your stomach: Jeg har kvalme.

hospital.note: Same word as in English, stressed on the end: hos-pi-TAL. Also: sygehus.

lost_phone.note: Casual: Jeg har mistet min mobil.

allergic.note: E.g. Jeg er allergisk over for nødder (nuts).

be_careful.note: Also: Forsigtig! When parting, take care: Pas godt på dig selv.

no_problem.note: After an apology, Danes often say Det gør ikke noget (it doesn't matter).

of_course.note: The v is silent: 'sel-FØL-yeh-lee'. Casual: Klart!

dont_know.note: Also: Jeg ved det ikke. Casual: Aner det ikke (no idea).

i_like_it.note: Lide sounds like 'LEE-eh'. Stronger: Jeg elsker det (I love it).

dont_like_it.note: The godt drops out in the negative.

im_happy.note: Glad is the everyday word for happy, not only 'glad'.

welcome.note: Hosts often add: Kom indenfor! (come in)

mother.note: Also what you call your own mum: Mor! Grandma: mormor (mum's side), farmor (dad's side).

father.note: Also what you call your own dad: Far! Grandpa: morfar (mum's side), farfar (dad's side).

brother.note: Plural: brødre. Big brother: storebror. Siblings: søskende.

sister.note: Plural: søstre. Big sister: storesøster. Little sister: lillesøster.

child.note: Plural: børn. Son: søn. Daughter: datter.

friend.note: A female friend: veninde. Boyfriend or girlfriend: kæreste.

this_is_my_friend.note: For a female friend: Det her er min veninde. Also common: Det er en ven af mig.

are_you_married.note: Many couples live together without marrying; a live-in partner is a samlever.

have_children.note: The ø is like the u in 'burn', with rounded lips. How many? Hvor mange børn har du?

monday.note: Days take a small letter. The g is silent: 'MAN-da'. On Monday: på mandag. On Mondays: om mandagen.

wednesday.note: Named after the god Odin. Roughly 'OANS-da'.

thursday.note: Named after Thor, the god of thunder.

friday.note: Roughly 'FRAY-da'. A cosy Friday night in with the family is fredagshygge.

saturday.note: The ø is like the u in 'burn': roughly 'LUR-da'.

sunday.note: On Sundays: om søndagen. This Sunday: på søndag.

weekend.note: This is the everyday Danish word. Have a nice weekend: God weekend!

what_day.text: Hvilken dag er det i dag?
what_day.note: Casual: Hvad dag er det i dag? The date: Hvad er datoen i dag?

next_week.note: The g in uge is silent: 'OO-eh'. Last week: i sidste uge. This week: i denne uge.

fifteen.note: The teens end in -ten: tretten (13), fjorten (14), seksten (16).

twenty.note: Danes put the ones first: 21 is enogtyve (one-and-twenty).

thirty.note: The i is silent: roughly 'TRATH-veh', with the d like th in 'this'.

fifty.note: Said 'hal-TRESS'. It comes from counting in twenties (2½ × 20). 60 is tres, 70 halvfjerds.

hundred.note: Also: et hundrede. Two hundred: to hundrede.

thousand.note: Also: et tusind. The d is silent: 'TOO-sen'. As in Tusind tak!

years_old.note: Also: Jeg er … år gammel. År sounds like 'or'.

red.note: The d is soft, like th in 'this'. With neuter nouns: rødt, e.g. et rødt hus.

blue.note: With neuter nouns: blåt. Light blue: lyseblå. Dark blue: mørkeblå.

green.note: With neuter nouns: grønt, e.g. et grønt æble.

yellow.note: Sounds like 'cool' with a g. With neuter nouns: gult.

black.note: Same form with neuter nouns: et sort hus.

white.note: The h is silent and the d soft: 'veeth'. With neuter nouns: hvidt.

what_colour.note: For a neuter noun: Hvilken farve er det? Also: Hvilken farve har den?

this_one.note: For a neuter noun: det her. Several items: de her.

that_one.note: For a neuter noun: det der. Further off: den derovre (that one over there).

another_one.note: For a neuter noun: et til. Also: Må jeg få en til?

its_hot.note: Varmt covers both warm and hot. A heatwave is a hedebølge.

its_cold.note: The d is silent: 'kolt'. Freezing: Det er iskoldt.

its_raining.note: Eg sounds like 'eye': roughly 'RYE-nah'. Pouring down: Det øsregner.

its_sunny.note: Also: Det er solskin i dag.

its_windy.note: Very windy, as a joke: Det blæser en halv pelikan.

weather_today.note: Vejr (weather) sounds like 'vair'. The forecast: vejrudsigten.

beautiful_day.note: Dejlig sounds like 'DYE-lee'. As an exclamation: Sikke en dejlig dag!

umbrella.note: Stress on the end: pa-ra-PLÜ, with the Danish y sound.

summer.note: In summer: om sommeren. Summer holidays: sommerferie.

have_reservation.note: Also: Jeg har bestilt et værelse (I've booked a room).

room.note: Double room: dobbeltværelse. Single room: enkeltværelse.

luggage.note: Said the French way: ba-GAY-sheh. Hand luggage: håndbagage.

wifi_password.note: Also: Hvad er koden til nettet? Kode is the everyday word for a password.

check_out_time.note: For a group: Hvornår skal vi tjekke ud? More formal: Hvornår er udtjekning?

map.note: Also means card, as in betale med kort. City map: bykort.

next_train.note: Tog (train) sounds like 'tow'. Also: Hvornår går næste tog?

is_this_seat_free.note: Very common: Sidder der nogen her? (is anyone sitting here?)

what_do_you_do.note: Also: Hvad laver du til daglig? Plain Hvad laver du? means what are you doing right now.

i_work_in.note: For a field, use med: Jeg arbejder med salg. Some places take på: på et hotel.

im_student.note: Same for a woman. Also: Jeg studerer. A school pupil is an elev.

office.note: Stress on the end: kon-TOR. At the office: på kontoret.

meeting.note: The d is soft, like th in 'this'. I'm in a meeting: Jeg sidder i møde.

im_busy.note: Danes use har (have) here, not er (am). Also: Jeg er optaget (I'm tied up).

day_off.note: I'm off today: Jeg har fri i dag.

colleague.note: Same for a woman. Plural: kolleger or kollegaer.

lets_start.note: Lad is said 'la'. As a question: Skal vi gå i gang?

good_job.note: Godt is said 'got'. Also: Flot klaret!

table_for_two.note: If you've booked: Vi har bestilt bord på navnet Jensen.

not_spicy.note: Stærk is the word for spicy (and strong). To ask: Er den stærk? Not too spicy: ikke for stærk.

vegetarian_food.note: Mad (food) has a soft d, like th in 'this'. Vegan: vegansk.

more_water.note: More politely: Må vi få noget mere vand? A jug of tap water: en kande vand.

im_full.note: Mæt rhymes with 'met'. Stuffed: Jeg er propmæt.

takeaway.note: Staff often ask: Spiser du her, eller skal det med? Takeaway food: mad ud af huset.

it_was_delicious.note: Warmer: Det var rigtig lækkert! At someone's home, say Tak for mad after eating.

keep_change.note: Tipping is not expected in Denmark, as service is included in the price.

head.note: The v is silent and the d soft: roughly 'HO-eth'.

stomach.note: My stomach hurts: Jeg har ondt i maven. A stomachache: mavepine.

head_hurts.note: Also: Jeg har hovedpine (a headache). Ondt i … works for any body part.

have_fever.note: Feber sounds like 'FAY-bah'. I have a cold: Jeg er forkølet.

medicine.note: Stress on the end: meh-dee-SEEN. Painkillers: smertestillende.

call_ambulance.note: Ring efter means call for someone to come; ring til is to phone someone. Emergency: 112.

dentist.note: Tand (tooth) + læge (doctor). The d is silent: 'TAN-lay-yeh'.

need_rest.text: Jeg har brug for at hvile mig
need_rest.note: Also: Jeg trænger til at hvile mig. The h in hvile is silent: 'VEE-leh'.

feel_better.note: Asking someone: Har du det bedre? Much better: meget bedre.

lets_meet.note: Plans are usually suggested as questions with skal vi. Also: Skal vi mødes en dag?

are_you_free.note: Casual: Kan du i morgen? Har du fri? asks if you are off work.

call_me.text: Du må gerne ringe til mig
call_me.note: Shorter: Ring til mig. Text me: Send mig en sms.

your_number.note: Shorter: Hvad er dit nummer? Asking for it: Må jeg få dit nummer?

see_you_soon.note: Casual: Ses snart! See you tomorrow: Vi ses i morgen.

have_nice_day.note: Hav sounds like 'how'. Reply: Tak, i lige måde! (same to you)

good_luck.note: Before an exam or a show, also: Knæk og bræk!

happy_birthday.note: The d in fødsel is silent. Casual: Tillykke!

thanks_a_lot.note: Even warmer: Tusind tak! Mange sounds like 'MANG-eh'.

miss_you.note: To several people: Jeg savner jer. Dig sounds like 'die'.
